title: 🌱 ThoughtTree design
note: Vision and goals: what ThoughtTree is for, in the owner's words and as quality goals. Source: [ux-concept.md](https://github.com/AdventureDevelopment/ThoughtTree/blob/main/docs/ux-concept.md), [architecture.md](https://github.com/AdventureDevelopment/ThoughtTree/blob/main/docs/architecture.md) section 1.

title: Vision in the owner's words
note:
> It's a structured thought trap. You have an idea, put it in there and sort it out now or later. Inspired by GTD: clear your mind, be sure everything is caught and processed later. Don't forget a thing and structure them as you wish. Work out details, be creative with your thinking, take notes from a speech or a meeting, put them in context now quickly, structure them afterwards. Structuring can lead to complex projects, not as tasks or todos, but as thoughts, which can evolve or spawn todos, appointments (mostly with myself to reserve time slots), delegation.

- Items grow: an idea becomes a project, a topic or a vision by working on it, without changing what it is in the app
- Spawning todos, appointments and delegations is part of the vision but not decided; it is exactly where the risk of drifting into task management begins (architecture section 11, "the MLO trap"); for the architecture and a later product decision

title: What the owner always wanted and never found
note:
Named by the owner after trying the first prototype (2026-11-13). These are the heart of ThoughtTree; when a decision is hard or a detail is unclear, they win:

- **Themes per branch:** every project or topic can carry its own mood, visible in the overview and filling the screen when focused
- **The inbox, always at hand:** the capture button is there everywhere, even while editing another item; the inbox has its own entry in the global menu with its full item menu; and it can have its own theme, like any branch (capturing itself is known from MLO's widgets; what is new is having the inbox at hand everywhere)
- **Markdown and emojis:** Markdown in titles (inline) and notes; emojis everywhere, also in tags and other names (tags and names stay unformatted)
- **Focus:** concentrating on one item and its branch as if it were its own document, in the branch's theme, with the title shown in full and editable in place, and back always returning to the previous view and position (named by the owner as another killer feature after trying the prototype)

title: Key requirements
note:
- Hierarchical (tree-based) notes with unlimited nesting, collapse/expand, drag-and-drop, focus on an item
- Runs on every device as an installable PWA
- Standalone first: a device works fully on its own, with no internet, no account and no server; pairing with other devices and server sync are optional and can be added later
- Synchronisation of items across devices over the internet
- Touch-first outliner UX for phone and tablet; keyboard shortcuts on desktop as a nice add-on
- End-to-end encrypted: notes are encrypted on the device before sync; the server never sees plaintext
- Fast full-text search across all notes, performed on the device (the server never sees plaintext)
- Direct device-to-device sync: two paired devices can exchange events with each other without going through the sync server
- Multiple trees per device: a device can hold several independent trees side by side, each with its own key and event log (for example a private and a work tree)
- See where changes come from: every device has a label (for example "Tablet"), and an item shows which device last changed it and when
- Explicit sharing: pairing another device of one's own and sharing a tree with another user are two separate actions; every tree shows whether it is private or shared, and with whom
- Usable where VPNs are blocked: file-only sync stays a full alternative, the user controls app updates, and the sync server can be self-hosted
- Readable export and import: a tree can be exported unencrypted as Markdown, OPML or JSON, and such files can be imported as a new tree or into an existing item
- Importing a tree into another: another tree can be imported into a tree as a new branch, keeping its history (union of their event logs, re-encrypted with this tree's key); the receiving tree keeps its name, theme and inbox; everyone who holds the receiving tree can then read the imported tree including its history
- Honest about protection: the app states plainly what it protects (content) and what it does not hide (that and when ThoughtTree is used)

title: Quality goals
note:
| Priority | Quality goal | Motivation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Reliability | No data loss, offline or during sync, merge, import, update or conflict; all devices with the same events and the same app version show the same tree; notes outlive app versions, frameworks and cloud services, so old data stays readable for good |
| 2 | Privacy & Security | Personal thoughts stay private: end-to-end encryption on the device, the server only relays ciphertext; minimal metadata, in particular nobody operating or observing the server learns where the user is; integrity of events |
| 3 | Usability | Outliner UX like MLO on touch devices: quick capture, drag-and-drop, gestures; keyboard on desktop; accessible (screen readers, keyboard-only use, contrast, scalable text); English and German; honest about what is protected |
| 4 | Portability | Runs on phone, tablet and desktop in all major browsers (Chromium-based, Safari, Firefox); installable as PWA, later as store app or package; server self-hostable without Azure; data never locked in (readable export and import) |
| 5 | Maintainability | Testable (replaceable time and randomness, device simulation); changeable without breaking stored data (downward-compatible events, format versions); manageable by one developer; one language (C#) across client and server |
| 6 | Performance | Trees with thousands of items stay responsive (targets in section 10) |

title: Stakeholders
note:
| Role | Expectation |
| --- | --- |
| Owner / developer (Sourceress) | A tool for personal thinking that is fun to build and maintain in C# |
| End users (initially the owner) | Reliable notes on phone, tablet and desktop |

title: 🧭 UX concept
note: Principles, terms, journeys and the decision log [D-1](item:f92ffb50-b86e-5f60-bc95-933beca12283) to [D-192](item:22635cbf-42bf-5dc9-8597-275c00bb17b8). Source: [ux-concept.md](https://github.com/AdventureDevelopment/ThoughtTree/blob/main/docs/ux-concept.md). Where code and a UX decision differ, the decision wins ([ADR-064](item:2b937f07-3185-55a9-9eb0-bc66af3e2a1d)).

title: UX principles
note: Derived from journeys A to D ([D-16](item:94f85396-f2fa-544c-914d-b711e60de01a), [D-24](item:784f3969-f376-5235-b0ff-7231e4f727ce)). They guide every later decision, including the agents'.

title: 1. Capture first, structure later
note: Nothing has to be decided before typing: not the place, not the tree, not the kind. ([D-1](item:f92ffb50-b86e-5f60-bc95-933beca12283), [D-4](item:61e74ffa-c6ec-5d64-9f0a-7b31e2ce4bf1), [D-5](item:a32e82dc-aeea-5131-b535-ecdecad75a4c))

title: 2. Create in the tree, go deeper in Focus
note: New items are created and named in place in the tree; titles take inline Markdown (emphasis, links, inline code) and emojis. Shortcuts live in the text itself (space, Backspace, `##`, `@@`), each with a visible alternative. Longer text is written in Focus on the item, which shows the thought as a page ([D-151](item:768c4ff2-e921-5d89-9ef9-d0eed2cd469a)). Quick capture opens a light sheet whose lines behave exactly like the outline, so typing works the same everywhere. ([D-2](item:5ee369d3-a9b1-5925-bc3d-f3c6e3d3b5d9), [D-3](item:55496035-7c23-53e7-a7b2-9ea191e85c76), [D-10](item:2a0c2a0e-53aa-51c7-a51e-764883f0472a), [D-11](item:eccafab5-71a3-5768-8806-889fcec7d645), [D-14](item:b34aea28-04c0-58d3-bf0d-d61fd3e436b6), [D-18](item:e3fc02be-f14d-5320-9504-e7ffff401c4f))

title: 3. Stay in the flow
note: After every action the user stays where they were, and the next step is right there. ([D-2](item:5ee369d3-a9b1-5925-bc3d-f3c6e3d3b5d9), [D-7](item:f0254a1d-536b-5cb1-a02a-710dcba5fd85), [D-13](item:9e6c7dfe-2e60-59be-9006-9af6309a5f11))

title: 4. Effort fits the distance
note: Near by hand (drag), far by choosing (search); finding the right place must be easy. ([D-6](item:6cb09e1e-6a0c-5e6a-a841-2274c0b1a8df), [D-9](item:e144671a-7f7e-55e4-98fc-c16f7e11a815))

title: 5. Calm, no pressure
note: No badges, no warning colours, no reminders that push. ([D-8](item:d427ea6c-82da-57cf-bcda-69a53deceb3c))

title: 6. Several dimensions
note: The tree is one order; tags and relations add more. ([D-13](item:9e6c7dfe-2e60-59be-9006-9af6309a5f11), [D-14](item:b34aea28-04c0-58d3-bf0d-d61fd3e436b6))

title: 7. Saved at once and reliably
note: The user never wonders whether something was stored. (Journey A; quality goal reliability)

title: 8. Start simple
note: A feature comes when use shows it is missed. ([D-9](item:e144671a-7f7e-55e4-98fc-c16f7e11a815), [D-15](item:872cf80c-85b9-5c40-b73f-65c9fc2f001d))

title: 9. Nothing happens behind the user's back
note: The app shows what arrived and what clashed, and never decides silently for the user; when something needs the user, it waits calmly until they have time. ([D-21](item:8816010b-86d1-5d62-8c45-a123360836dd), [D-22](item:c92c9231-8858-5894-bdf3-5ed893cb79eb), [D-23](item:c409cbbe-2e1f-5cd5-9335-84af5d3c8ca2); [ADR-018](item:145e6add-bf20-5378-a075-0ef31b6a908d))

title: 10. Your own thinking
note: ThoughtTree has no AI that reads, structures or writes your thoughts. The structure grows from your own decisions: deciding where a thought belongs and how thoughts connect is the thinking itself, and some thoughts are for nobody else. That is the point, not a missing feature. ([D-142](item:083977dc-8cea-547c-9ae6-845452d1d620); [ADR-071](item:1bc7e63d-dcfc-5adb-87b2-dc10128daf48), Accepted)

title: Terms
note:
This concept uses the following terms (decision [D-45](item:ec0ed326-4a12-50f8-8564-6c575e213459), replacing [D-44](item:43ea7b38-cf8a-508c-9259-1e4e90116353)). The architecture adopted them with [ADR-063](item:b37c4ccc-f367-50df-9119-c3ba2f6da5e5) (Accepted); "Focus" instead of "Zoom" with [ADR-065](item:37387329-c750-5cd5-9367-9f45ee092e98) (Accepted).

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Tree | One independent outline with its own key and event log, for example "Private" or "Work" |
| Item | The thing in the tree: a title, a note, tags, and optionally a theme and views; later also pictures and files. What it is (a thought, an idea, a seed, a project, a topic, a vision) is the user's to decide, for example with tags; an item can grow |
| Thought | The user-facing word for an item: the app's texts say thought(s) ([D-140](item:4fec508f-8d98-5cf1-9104-57384c68e905), [D-161](item:7307644b-3f89-5160-a9ba-a509b2f7c0d5) "Gedanke"); item stays the technical term in documents, code and tests ([ADR-063](item:b37c4ccc-f367-50df-9119-c3ba2f6da5e5)) |
| Note | The optional longer text of an item, written in Focus on the item ([D-151](item:768c4ff2-e921-5d89-9ef9-d0eed2cd469a)) |
| Branch | An item together with everything below it |
| Node | How an item appears in the tree: its line in the outline and its place; a technical term for code and specifications |
| Focus | Make an item the temporary top of the view, showing its branch and the item as a page: title, tags and note ([D-57](item:0b14f20b-fccf-5776-a31d-86c9d71d3b0a), [D-151](item:768c4ff2-e921-5d89-9ef9-d0eed2cd469a), [ADR-065](item:37387329-c750-5cd5-9367-9f45ee092e98), [ADR-072](item:62d06ce7-f9af-581e-9fad-86105c54e5a3)) |

What the app calls these things in its own wording is decided with microcopy (topic 10).

title: Journeys
note: Four situations the concept was derived from.

title: Journey A: The idea on waking
note:
The owner wakes up in bed, still half asleep; an idea comes up that must not be lost. Phone, probably one hand.

1. Opens ThoughtTree from the home screen; it shows the place last worked on, with the bottom toolbar and its capture button 📥 in the middle (decisions [D-4](item:61e74ffa-c6ec-5d64-9f0a-7b31e2ce4bf1), [D-17](item:5dd2ea73-09c2-55d9-9aee-273afefe4d04))
2. Taps 📥: a light sheet slides up over the dimmed current view, with an empty line, the keyboard and the name of the target tree (decision [D-18](item:e3fc02be-f14d-5320-9504-e7ffff401c4f))
3. Types the title right away, often starting with an emoji
4. **Key moment:** the idea is saved; from now on nothing can be lost
5. Optionally adds context: a note and a tag
6. If it is a chain of ideas, enters the next idea right away, without detours
7. Closes the sheet and is back where they were
8. Where the idea belongs in the tree is decided later, not now

Remarks:

- The idea lands in an inbox (decision [D-1](item:f92ffb50-b86e-5f60-bc95-933beca12283)); no decision about its place is needed before typing
- The next idea of a chain is a sibling; a space typed into its empty title nests it under the previous idea (decision [D-2](item:5ee369d3-a9b1-5925-bc3d-f3c6e3d3b5d9))
- Backspace in an empty title moves it one level up; at the top level of the inbox it removes the empty line (decision [D-3](item:55496035-7c23-53e7-a7b2-9ea191e85c76))
- The capture view shows the tree the idea goes into (the open tree); one tap switches to another tree (decision [D-5](item:a32e82dc-aeea-5131-b535-ecdecad75a4c))
- Inside the app, capture happens directly in the outline: a new line in the tree, typed in place; there is one way of entering titles, the note is written in Focus on the item (decisions [D-10](item:2a0c2a0e-53aa-51c7-a51e-764883f0472a), [D-151](item:768c4ff2-e921-5d89-9ef9-d0eed2cd469a))
- Fast typers write `Title ## Note` in one go; what follows `##` becomes the item's note (decision [D-11](item:eccafab5-71a3-5768-8806-889fcec7d645))
- The light capture sheet of MLO comes from its home-screen widget; a PWA cannot offer widgets, so this waits for the later store app or package; until then app shortcuts (press and hold the app icon: "New idea", Android and Windows only, not iPhone) are an option to consider
- Tags are added while typing with `@@` (decision [D-14](item:b34aea28-04c0-58d3-bf0d-d61fd3e436b6))
- Emojis in titles are already supported (section 8, text)
- Design target U1 (new item within two taps of opening the app) applies directly

Principle candidates heard in this journey (to be confirmed with the other journeys):

- Capture before order: writing comes first, sorting later
- No friction when half awake: no decision before typing
- Keep the flow: one idea leads to the next without detours
- Saved at once and reliably: the user never wonders whether something was stored

title: Journey B: Sorting with coffee
note:
The next morning the owner has made a coffee and drinks it in bed; awake, relaxed, with time. Phone in one hand, coffee in the other.

1. Opens the inbox with the ideas of the night
2. Sorts them one by one into the tree, choosing the way of moving by distance (decision [D-6](item:6cb09e1e-6a0c-5e6a-a841-2274c0b1a8df)):
   - next to another item nearby: drag and drop
   - into a project the owner has in mind: "Move to…", choose the project, see what is already there, place the idea where it belongs
   - something new: its own root, or wherever it belongs
3. After each move the owner stays in the inbox; a short confirmation shows where the idea went, with Undo and Go there (decision [D-7](item:f0254a1d-536b-5cb1-a02a-710dcba5fd85))
4. **Key moment:** the next idea belongs to the same project: one tap places it right below the idea just moved, no searching again (decision [D-7](item:f0254a1d-536b-5cb1-a02a-710dcba5fd85))
5. Stops when the mind is empty of ideas, not when the inbox is empty; ideas may stay in the inbox for a while (decision [D-8](item:d427ea6c-82da-57cf-bcda-69a53deceb3c))

Pain point: searching for the place where a new item belongs. In MLO the target picker offers fixed targets (inbox, top and bottom of the root level), the five targets last used for moving, and browsing the whole tree, but no search; a target outside the recent five means digging through the tree. Answered by the target picker (decision [D-9](item:e144671a-7f7e-55e4-98fc-c16f7e11a815)).

Remarks:

- A swipe on an idea as a shortcut to "Move to…" was a wish; the swipe on a row now does Focus ([D-72](item:d86e9795-02a6-5cad-ab6f-1ab669372cfc), [D-151](item:768c4ff2-e921-5d89-9ef9-d0eed2cd469a)), so "Move to…" stays in the item menu for now

Principle candidates heard in journey B:

- The way of acting fits the distance: near by hand, far by choosing
- Stay in the flow: after an action the user stays where they were
- No pressure: the inbox is a parking place, not a to-do list
- Finding the place is the hard part; the app must make it easy
- Start simple: features nobody has missed yet (for example pinned places) wait until use shows the need

title: Journey C: I know there was something
note:
The owner is planning something and knows there are already items about it somewhere in the tree; one word is remembered.

1. Starts a search and types the word
2. **Key moment:** the tree itself is filtered: only the matching items and their parents stay visible, the word is highlighted (decision [D-12](item:dfcd32f4-c91f-56b1-9d28-aeffcf1b1b62))
3. Links the found items to the plan instead of moving them; they stay where they are and the plan points to them (decision [D-13](item:9e6c7dfe-2e60-59be-9006-9af6309a5f11))
4. Stays in the filtered view after linking and continues with the next match [ASSUMPTION, by analogy with [D-7](item:f0254a1d-536b-5cb1-a02a-710dcba5fd85)]

Principle candidate heard in journey C and in the wish for tags: several dimensions for items; the tree is one order (where an item belongs), tags and relations add more (what kind, which context, which status, what it relates to).

title: Journey D: From phone to tablet, offline
note:
The owner has captured ideas on the phone and wants to continue on the tablet; there is no internet at all.

1. Captured ideas on the phone
2. Wants to continue with them on the tablet
3. Hands the changes from the phone to the tablet as an encrypted file ([ADR-007](item:72d8232b-5c71-5140-9596-9e03184d4407); decision [D-19](item:3751984b-f329-5796-9dc4-2434cdf36c72))
4. The tablet reads the file in and offers right away to send its own changes back; one more transfer and both devices are equal (decision [D-20](item:179e0e5b-74db-5dfe-a978-d4b147c04f03))
5. **Key moment:** wants to continue with the items that just arrived; a short confirmation names how many arrived and offers Show, which filters the tree to them (decision [D-21](item:8816010b-86d1-5d62-8c45-a123360836dd))
6. An item changed on both devices while offline is named in the confirmation ("1 conflict") and marked on the item until it is resolved (decision [D-22](item:c92c9231-8858-5894-bdf3-5ed893cb79eb))
7. Resolves it: a small, unconnected item by picking a version or writing a new one; an item connected to many things only after looking at its context again (decision [D-23](item:c409cbbe-2e1f-5cd5-9335-84af5d3c8ca2))

Remarks:

- Sync over the local Wi-Fi is not possible for a PWA by local discovery; a direct WebRTC connection with a handshake by QR codes, without a server, would be possible but needs an ADR (Content Security Policy, [ADR-045](item:4ed194a5-683a-5f25-9867-341f6922bd57)) and a spike; kept as an idea for later, besides the native wrapper with local discovery named in the architecture

title: Undo (topic 2)
note:
The owner thinks of undo like a git repository: every change is a commit that is never erased, and undo is a revert (decision [D-25](item:4b49ca2d-8883-5097-8626-ab3999cd72c2)).

| Need | Git equivalent | In ThoughtTree |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reverse the last slip | `git revert HEAD` | Undo right after the action (also in the confirmation after a move, [D-7](item:f0254a1d-536b-5cb1-a02a-710dcba5fd85)) |
| Step back several actions | Several reverts | Undo button or Ctrl+Z, repeated, through the user's own actions on this device |
| Go back much later | `git log`, restore a file | The item's history: every version with device and time, any change revertible, whoever made it |

- Quick undo does not go strictly by time: with live sync, a change from another device can arrive between the user's action and the undo; undoing that instead of the user's own slip would be surprising
- Undo is not limited to the current view (changing the focus would lose it, and a move belongs to two places); instead undo always shows what it reverses
- While text is being edited, it is a local draft ([ADR-013](item:2503cff6-630e-5fbd-89f6-22dd074fee11)): the editor's usual undo and redo apply within the draft, character by character or word by word; once editing ends, the whole text change is one step for quick undo; for all other actions there is undo but no redo, a regretted undo is reverted from the history (decision [D-26](item:2ed08a3b-769f-54ca-90f6-81429784abc0))
- Quick undo needs no list of its own: it is read from the log (this device's events, newest first); an undo event names the event it reverts, like git's "This reverts commit …", so the history can show "reverted by …" and undo survives closing the app (decision [D-27](item:817f2dda-de33-569c-ab91-7acb6e906edd))
- When the item was changed since on another device or by another user, quick undo stops and asks instead of overwriting: "This item has been changed since on Tablet ('C'). Open history?" (decision [D-28](item:2fce5f30-46e4-5b0c-9dde-27fc7e6f2238))
- Quick undo reaches back without limit; since every undo shows what it reverses, an old step cannot happen unnoticed (decision [D-29](item:14d98262-fee2-5060-b6da-4679ebb8e61d))
- Architecture change proposed as [ADR-059](item:23cd8632-6a91-51e3-9452-e5d6907a66d0) (Accepted); the item history brings forward what the architecture names as "possible later"

title: Component library (topic 3)
note:
The library is chosen by a spike (decision [D-30](item:c6dafc1b-9138-5c7a-b930-a9d163fcc440)).

- Candidates: MudBlazor, Fluent UI Blazor, Radzen Blazor (all MIT), and own components; commercial libraries (Telerik, Syncfusion, DevExpress) are excluded by the licence rule ([ADR-050](item:27268cd1-2dc2-519f-a69f-99bad621e0f1))
- The spike also checks the libraries' tree components (MudTreeView, FluentTreeView, RadzenTree): whether one can carry the outliner or serve as its base
- Criteria:
  - works under the strict Content Security Policy without `unsafe-inline` ([ADR-045](item:4ed194a5-683a-5f25-9867-341f6922bd57))
  - accessible: no axe findings, keyboard only, screen readers ([ADR-033](item:75be0950-c5ca-5362-8542-42881e719183))
  - direction-neutral: CSS logical properties, works mirrored ([ADR-033](item:75be0950-c5ca-5362-8542-42881e719183))
  - download size within the budget (PF5)
  - themeable through our own design tokens, light and dark (topic 4), far enough to carry ThoughtTree's own calm look instead of the library's ([D-31](item:994fa1d9-49a2-5a53-9092-a51be7cc1276))
  - touch targets of at least 24×24 CSS pixels ([ADR-033](item:75be0950-c5ca-5362-8542-42881e719183))
  - for the note: an editor that formats Markdown as you type, converts pasted HTML to Markdown cleanly, is accessible and works in both writing directions ([D-61](item:3d4b82a1-e252-59f6-8375-d2611145d205))
  - for the tree component: typing in place with Enter, leading space and Backspace ([D-2](item:5ee369d3-a9b1-5925-bc3d-f3c6e3d3b5d9), [D-3](item:55496035-7c23-53e7-a7b2-9ea191e85c76)), the `##` and `@@` shortcuts ([D-11](item:eccafab5-71a3-5768-8806-889fcec7d645), [D-14](item:b34aea28-04c0-58d3-bf0d-d61fd3e436b6)), 10,000 items stay responsive (PF1, PF2), dragging with an accessible alternative ([D-6](item:6cb09e1e-6a0c-5e6a-a841-2274c0b1a8df))

title: Design tokens and theming (topic 4)
note:
- Reference for the look: MyLifeOrganized (light, plain, a fresh accent colour), in ThoughtTree's own calm look ([D-31](item:994fa1d9-49a2-5a53-9092-a51be7cc1276))
- The first theme is calm; more colourful themes may come later, so tokens are semantic (for example `surface`, `text`, `accent`, `conflict-marker`), and a theme only swaps the palette behind them (decision [D-32](item:b9c7f112-7566-5c58-a54e-8e7af6f42fa8))
- First theme: **Paper**, warm paper tones with a rust ochre accent (decision [D-33](item:998fbe7e-11a6-58a9-a589-46a52b9ed481)); compared against Fresh, Slate and Quiet mono, and against a terracotta, a burnt sienna and a warm brown accent

| Token (draft) | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `surface` (page, bars) | `#f7f3ec` | `#1c1915` |
| `surface-content` (list) | `#fffdf8` | `#23201b` |
| `text` | `#2a2520` | `#ece5da` |

- Themes can be chosen per tree and per item, to support the vibe of a project; an item's theme applies to its whole branch (shown for all its children, unless a child has its own theme), and shows when the user focuses on it (decision [D-34](item:cd0c6b92-ccc2-539a-9123-bcb1de7ee943))
- In the overview a branch with its own theme is tinted in that theme, so its mood is visible before focusing on it; focused on it, the whole screen takes on the theme (decision [D-35](item:76c1ff04-aac3-50c6-9a44-ed71e79d4ded); sketch: dot versus tinted branch versus focused)
- Themes of trees and branches are shared: the same on every device and for every user of a tree, recorded by an event; proposed as [ADR-060](item:bf684b01-1e00-5613-b339-982fb1ed2313) (Accepted) (decision [D-36](item:5430cc3b-6ce6-5bee-a99b-0f17a66f36fa))
- Typography: the base font is the device's system font, so startup downloads nothing; a theme may bring its own font (for example Literata for writing, Nunito for creative, IBM Plex Mono for technical projects), downloaded in the background after start and kept offline; proposed as [ADR-061](item:acf46933-f26e-5b3d-b2ba-1d9510e0ba2a) (Accepted), which also approves the SIL Open Font License for fonts (decision [D-37](item:bf9e8fd4-9324-5773-b833-f1300742fb6b))
- Custom views: views belong to an item (decision [D-39](item:2f9a2ce2-ed4c-5e0a-8d34-a9eca53f49f3), revising [D-38](item:38321d20-aa15-5504-9066-4be7bbb3d8e0)):
  - every item, and the tree itself, can carry one or more views; the default is the outline
  - a view is a saved search over the item's branch (for example "🔎 Open questions", "Changed recently") and, later, a layout such as a board or columns
  - views are reached through 🔍 Search, not at the top ([D-125](item:ab0ed42e-f1da-529f-9302-dc7c8ef1e116)); the item's theme applies to all its views
  - at the tree level, a view "All views" lists every view of the tree with the path of its item
  - the start view of a device is an item plus one of its views
  - start icons with their own view (decision [D-40](item:fa21f518-ec95-5c77-aa68-0889875f30da)): the app understands a start parameter "item plus view" in its address from the start; Android: "Add to home screen" from such a link (spike: does it open in the app window or a tab); Windows and desktop: links with the start parameter; iPhone and iPad: with the store app, because each home-screen web app there has its own storage
  - proposed as [ADR-062](item:3ecc302d-7862-5524-8174-9dff17cce88a) (Accepted)
- A theme brings more than colours: palette, optionally a font ([D-37](item:bf9e8fd4-9324-5773-b833-f1300742fb6b)), the density of the outline and whether the first line of an item's note is previewed under its title. Paper: density comfortable (rows about 44 px, text 16 px, system font) with the note preview shown (decision [D-42](item:a196f4fd-ad26-509b-a8b1-3f2ef312645e); sketch: airy, comfortable, compact)
- Text size follows the device: the theme's sizes are the starting point, and the device's text-size setting scales them (sizes in relative units; on iPhone and iPad the system text style is used so Dynamic Type applies); rows grow with the text, layouts must hold at 200 % text size; no slider of its own in the app (decision [D-43](item:ddf77d48-821d-59ef-afc8-8a0d5d8ec3da))
- **Signature feature:** a theme for a part of the tree, tinted in the overview and taking over the whole screen when focused on; the owner has not seen this anywhere else

All text and accent pairs above meet WCAG AA contrast; the contrast unit test (architecture section 8) will check them once they are code.

title: UX with agents (topic 11)
note:
How the owner's UX intent reaches the agents, and how the owner checks the result (decision [D-46](item:e4313538-bd80-5421-a1cf-cb2fb80be671)):

- Before: for a new screen or a visibly new part of one, the agent first makes an HTML sketch (as in this concept: variants side by side, real wording, Paper theme); the owner chooses or corrects it; only then the agent writes the UI specification and the code
- The owner does not approve UI specifications separately beforehand; changes to specifications are reviewed anyway in the pull request, because `tests/specify/**` is a protected path (architecture section 2)
- After: the pull request shows screenshots generated from the UI specifications, for phone and tablet, light and dark
- After: the owner tries the feature in the test environment on their own devices, through a link in the pull request
- Example content in sketches, specifications and test data consists of thoughts (ideas, questions, observations, projects as thoughts), never of tasks or todos, matching the vision (decision [D-67](item:c9811840-ee58-5726-9e44-e58de5c9959d))
- Sketches are shown as artifacts for choosing; only the chosen variant is kept in the repository as reference, in `docs/ux/sketches/`, linked from its decision; rejected variants are not kept; where a sketch and the text of this concept differ, the text wins (decision [D-47](item:41d8579a-79f7-5bcd-b357-8549b5d5ba45))
- Binding, as a definition of done for UI work, by three means together (decision [D-48](item:25c1bffe-c9f3-5374-b0f5-2b22801f7288)): a rule for agents, proposed as [ADR-064](item:2b937f07-3185-55a9-9eb0-bc66af3e2a1d) (Accepted); a UI checklist in the pull request template; and a pointer to the UX concept in the agents' entry file (`CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`). Both exist: the UI checklist in `.github/pull_request_template.md` and the pointer in `AGENTS.md` (read through `CLAUDE.md`)

Definition of done for UI work (decision [D-49](item:98550057-ac06-51ab-be0e-72806386fe7e)): a UI feature is done when all three hold:

| Part | What it covers | Checked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Push gate (exists) | All tests, UI specifications, accessibility scans and ADR checks are green; [ADR-064](item:2b937f07-3185-55a9-9eb0-bc66af3e2a1d)'s automatable rules (tokens only, every UI specification names a UX decision) | CI |
| Pull request checklist ([D-48](item:25c1bffe-c9f3-5374-b0f5-2b22801f7288)) | What cannot be automated: principles checked, terms used, sketch linked, screenshots attached, keyboard and screen reader paths covered | The agent fills it, the owner checks it |
| Design review ([D-46](item:e4313538-bd80-5421-a1cf-cb2fb80be671)) | The owner looks at the screenshots, tries the feature in the test environment and approves | The owner |

19. Should a typed `[[` link also create a relation (for example of one built-in type "mentions"), so there is one kind of connection instead of two? Today the architecture keeps them apart on purpose (links are text, relations are deliberate). Postponing is safe: links keep the same form in the text either way, so a later version can read existing links as relations without rewriting content (cost then: a new ADR, a change in the projection, updated Links and Linked from; in shared trees older app versions show plain links until updated). The reverse would be hard, since relation events once written stay in every log. Belongs together with the open link part of templates ([D-111](item:c02be8a0-a23a-506d-995e-675115dac660)) and with whether predefined relation types are still needed in new trees or can move to the tutorial like the templates (owner's thought; [ADR-025](item:17b19d42-fcfc-57b1-b5aa-da9f2de567bd)). Partly settled in the architecture (2026-11-17, Zettelkasten decision 2, [zettelkasten-claim.md](https://github.com/AdventureDevelopment/ThoughtTree/blob/main/docs/zettelkasten-claim.md)): links stay text and are not turned into relations; the connection map draws them as untyped connections next to the relations, without events; the sketch question is in the architecture's open decision "Connection map (follow-ups)". The predefined types were settled on 2026-11-19 ([ADR-084](item:705c6e4b-83f7-5842-beb8-170c019a04e2), Proposed): a new tree gets only `related`, the tutorial offers further types to copy

Item menu and the menu in Focus ([D-167](item:e6dd9723-797d-59ba-8287-af8ae19c563a), deferred 2026-11-19 until the owner has tried the simplest form):

20. How the item menu stays short with about 14 entries, and what the focused thought's menu holds. Sketch: [item-menu-length.html](https://github.com/AdventureDevelopment/ThoughtTree/blob/main/docs/ux/sketches/item-menu-length.html). Variants: A one flat list in groups (built first, [D-167](item:e6dd9723-797d-59ba-8287-af8ae19c563a)); C six labelled tiles (Focus, Map, Move to…, Link to…, Tags, Theme) above a short list, with a dimmed "Focused" tile in Focus so the tiles keep their places; D in Focus, a panel grown from the line under the heading (History · Links · Linked from · Map · ▾ Actions) with ▾ Actions holding Move to…, Theme, Copy, Export…, Import into this thought… and Delete. Findings from the discussion: two buttons both named "⋯ More" on one screen confuse (hence "▾ Actions"); in Focus, Paste below lands outside the visible branch, Sort is covered by the move icon on every heading ([D-155](item:04fbcfd6-9f88-5c63-9285-73811e1a7c7b)), Views by 🔍 Search ([D-125](item:ab0ed42e-f1da-529f-9302-dc7c8ef1e116)), Link to… by the Links sheet ([D-85](item:3462a86f-6e98-590c-9c78-973032972215), with Links shown even at 0); moving the focused thought is rare and needs no button of its own; the bar's More › Paste at the top level could paste inside the focused thought while in Focus

Store app (for the architecture):

9. Native wrapper: .NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid looks like the most fitting route (same Razor components in C#, native shortcuts, widgets, background sync and shared-file sync; browser adapters swapped thanks to [ADR-042](item:808d9792-d2f3-5a38-b0ef-6a0f94c3d6ae)); alternatives Capacitor and PWABuilder/TWA; Apple's minimum-functionality review and developer accounts to consider. Not decided here

title: D-151 Focus replaces Open
note:
Focus replaces Open: there is no separate detail page any more, on any device. title: D-155 In Focus, the thoughts inside are formatted like headings, each with its note under it and deeper thoughts as smaller headings, so the page …
note:
In Focus, the thoughts inside are formatted like headings, each with its note under it and deeper thoughts as smaller headings, so the page reads like a document (Word's outline view); a small ● or ▾ in front marks them as thoughts. A heading is a thought: typing a heading in the note (`## …` or the H button) shows a hint ("↵ new thought inside") and on Enter becomes the first thought inside, the text after it moving into its note; nothing jumps on the page; a message offers Undo. Notes therefore hold no headings. Pasting or importing text with headings asks once: "Turn headings into thoughts" or "Keep as one note" (then the headings stay as bold lines). Moving on the page: every heading carries the light four-arrow move icon ([D-88](item:56cfdba4-6be3-5c33-a95a-fa90aae8ef4b)), shown whenever the user is not typing, so it is clear that each thought can be moved; tapping it switches to the flat outline without notes in sort mode (band "Sorting", grips, checkboxes) with that thought picked, and Done returns to the page at the moved thought. A long press on text always selects text [ASSUMPTION: dragging the move icon itself starts a drag at once, the notes folding while it lasts]. Proposed as [ADR-072](item:62d06ce7-f9af-581e-9fad-86105c54e5a3) (Proposed). Sketch: focus page (frames 1 to 4)

title: D-160 Tone rules
note:
Tone rules: (1) calm and plain: short sentences that say what is, no exclamation marks; (2) no cheerfulness on demand ("Oops!", "Yay!", "Great job!", "Awesome"); (3) no blame and no alarm: what happened, what is safe, what can be done ([D-128](item:48f7319e-d1ab-59a5-b30a-6b3c7f9aac12)); (4) no pressure: no "Don't miss…", "You should…", counts of things undone, streaks; (5) say it once: no confirmation questions for what can be undone, a message with Undo is enough ([D-99](item:28f1cdfb-e65a-59a8-9a6d-6d123f3b3238)); (6) in the app's own texts (buttons, menus, messages) emojis mark and do not decorate: one on a button or at the start of a label, none inside sentences; in the tutorial, where the tone is more personal, emojis are allowed more generously; (7) the same word for the same thing everywhere: thought, tree, branch, Focus, inbox, view, template

title: D-162 (1) Sentence case everywhere (German
note:
(1) Sentence case everywhere (German: normal German capitalisation). (2) "…" after a label means a further step follows before anything happens ("Move to…", "New view…"); without it the action happens at once ("Copy", "Delete"). title: D-163 Button texts chosen one by one by the owner
note:
Button texts chosen one by one by the owner. Pasting text with headings: "Turn headings into thoughts" · "Keep as one note". A file from a different tree: "Open as its own tree" · "Don't add". Feedback question: "Yes, offer me feedback" · "Not now" (a leading Yes strengthens a decision of consent). Conflict: "Keep as it is". Tutorial: "Remove the tutorial" · "Keep it". Removing a tree: "Remove from this device" · "Keep it here". New tree: "Create". New view: "Save as view". Changing a view's search: "Save changes" · "Discard changes". Sort mode: "Done". Sheets close with ✕ (spoken name "Close"). Messages: "Undo". Reminder to export: "Make a copy now". Storage almost full: "Help" (the owner's own word). Overlaps after an exchange: "Show both versions". Feedback line: "Something not right? Send feedback". Changed recently: "Show 5 more" · "Show fewer". Search without results: "Widen the search". Empty view and view menu: "Change its search". Link preview and the details column on wide screens: "Focus" (replaces "⤢ Give it room"). Theme picker's first entry: "No theme of its own" (the picker still names the theme it follows; replaces "Same as above", [D-65](item:b40dc4fc-3f99-5a6e-b894-cbcdf6596e6a)). More › Trees: "Bring the tutorial back". Rule drawn from the choices: where a button decides between outcomes it names the outcome, and the second button may name the other outcome ("Keep it", "Keep it here", "Discard changes", "Don't add"); a leading "Yes" marks consent; short words (Create, Done, Undo, Help) are fine where the context says the rest; never just OK

title: D-175 The note on a relation (ADR-077) as the user sees it
note:
The note on a relation ([ADR-077](item:b8470a09-0a1d-557c-97cf-a2370565e1d7)) as the user sees it: the reason why two thoughts are connected. (1) Wherever a relation is listed (the Links and Linked from sheet of [D-85](item:3462a86f-6e98-590c-9c78-973032972215), the map's card of [D-169](item:2f17bb50-b4e1-505d-93ed-b9f8c77c1399) and side column of [D-168](item:a048a86e-8297-5808-be07-788bad3b4dd0)), its reason shows under it in muted type, at most two lines; a relation without a reason shows only a small ＋ at the end of its row (accessible name "Add a reason"). (2) A reason is the exception, so nothing asks for it: Link to… links at once with the type `related` ([D-13](item:9e6c7dfe-2e60-59be-9006-9af6309a5f11)), and the message offers only Undo. (3) Tapping ＋ or a relation's ⋯ opens the relation sheet, one place per connection: from, a type chip, to (read left to right); the type chip opens the list of types with their reverse names and "＋ New type…" (closes the type part of gap G2); below, "Why are they connected?" written like a note (Markdown without headings, saved as you type, its own history and undo, [ADR-077](item:b8470a09-0a1d-557c-97cf-a2370565e1d7)); "Remove this connection" set apart, undone with Undo, the reason coming back with it; ✕ or ✓ closes. (4) On the map, tapping a line or its type label selects the connection: the line is drawn thicker in the accent colour and the card or side column shows from → type → to with the reason or ＋, and ⋯ opens the relation sheet; a dashed link shows the sentence around it instead (a link is text, with no type or reason); a line's tap area is at least 24 px wide ([ADR-033](item:75be0950-c5ca-5362-8542-42881e719183)); no reason text is drawn on the lines. (5) Screen readers hear the reason after the relation ("Supported by Spaced repetition. Reason: …", or "No reason" with the button "Add a reason"); on the map, keyboard and screen readers reach a connection through the thought at its end ([D-172](item:f15cf5af-fbc8-5a92-8401-d024dc1d5a10)), whose announcement includes type and reason. title: D-180 The readable import and export flow
note:
The readable import and export flow. (1) Export sheet: the thought or tree and its number of thoughts, the format (Obsidian as folders, Obsidian as flat files with "up", one Markdown document, OPML, JSON), the form of the last export preselected and marked "as last time" ([ADR-078](item:77cb2789-955d-5774-ad8d-96da9c92986e)). (2) Warning ([ADR-019](item:ffcefe90-c6a9-5c6a-b05b-325df4472983)): the first readable export on a device shows the full warning (not encrypted, anyone with the file can read every thought, keep it where only you can reach it and delete it when no longer needed; history, deleted thoughts and devices are not included) with a box to tick; every later export shows one line "🔓 Not encrypted: anyone with the file can read it · What this means", and the button "Export unencrypted" is the confirmation. (3) After the export a message names the file, whose name says UNENCRYPTED; no Undo (an export records a fact, [ADR-078](item:77cb2789-955d-5774-ad8d-96da9c92986e)). (4) "＋ Import a tree…" ([D-179](item:5476deb6-f093-5465-a88a-4afb5fa14368)) opens a sheet to choose a zip, Markdown files or a ThoughtTree export, and a folder where the browser allows it, with the hint to compress a vault in Files on iPad and iPhone. (5) The app reads the files first and proposes, with counts: the tree's name; what builds the tree (folders, the "up" property, Luhmann ids; the most used preselected, claim decision 4a); "Folder names as tags" ([ADR-082](item:f593841b-7318-58f3-8ca0-6f42beea0253)), shown only when folders do not build the tree and then on by default; headings in notes, "Keep them as headings" (as in Obsidian, switches the tree feature off for this tree, [ADR-079](item:89a6dcae-9f47-5920-907f-e286526addb2)) or "Turn them into thoughts"; which files will not be imported. (6) Importing shows a progress band with Cancel; nothing is added until all notes are in, Cancel leaves everything as it was; the new tree opens, the "🧾 Import report" is a thought at the end of the imported branch, a message offers "Open the report" and Undo (one undo step, acceptance scenario 12). (7) "Import into this thought…" with files that carry ids of this tree suggests "Update from these files" with counts (changed, new, missing) besides "Import as a copy"; files without ids are always a copy and the choice does not show. (8) After an update a message names what changed, conflicts and missing files, with Report and Undo; a change made in the app since the export becomes a conflict mark ([D-127](item:d80cde70-f754-5d09-8511-7c7e852a77bb)); a thought whose file is missing is only listed in the report with "Delete 1 thought whose file is missing…", which asks first; unchanged files write nothing and the message says "Nothing changed". title: D-181 Before release 1, an update that changes the stored format (ADR-085) is announced by a lasting banner (D-128 level 2)
note:
Before release 1, an update that changes the stored format ([ADR-085](item:30ed9a2b-2231-599a-8304-9a5a8d14fb7a)) is announced by a lasting banner ([D-128](item:48f7319e-d1ab-59a5-b30a-6b3c7f9aac12) level 2): "A new version is ready. It changes how thoughts are stored. · Before you update"; nothing updates on its own ([ADR-036](item:7db9fef2-7ffe-5038-beb0-ca224f3a3da7)); an ordinary update says only "A new version is ready · Update". "Before you update" opens a sheet that says the new version cannot open the current trees, that they stay on the device untouched, and that exporting brings thoughts, structure, notes, tags and connections along as far as possible, without history and conflicts; every tree is ticked except the tutorial (which comes back new); the export is one zip with a folder per tree in the Obsidian form, with the warning of [D-180](item:697fb705-44d7-553c-8d7d-0b5261f60df1); buttons "Export n trees unencrypted", "Update without exporting…" (asks once more, naming what will not open) and "Later" (keeps the banner). After the export, "Ready to update" names the saved file and offers "Update now". After the update, the tree list shows the old trees faded with "not readable by this version" (not opened, not changed) and "＋ Import your exported trees…" while old trees exist; the import recognises the app's own zip and creates each ticked tree as a new tree without asking about folders or headings, with progress and report as in [D-180](item:697fb705-44d7-553c-8d7d-0b5261f60df1), then offers to remove the old trees ("Remove from this device" · "Keep it here", [D-163](item:8514fcd4-cbb8-5b2f-9ca6-bd5836fecc32)). Not chosen: one file per tree. Sketch: beta format change

title: 🏛 Architecture (arc42)
note: The twelve arc42 sections of [architecture.md](https://github.com/AdventureDevelopment/ThoughtTree/blob/main/docs/architecture.md). Section 9's ADR index and open decisions are the branches "Decisions (ADRs)" and "Open decisions".

title: 1. Introduction and Goals
note: ThoughtTree is a hierarchical note-taking Progressive Web App for structuring thoughts as an outline tree. It is inspired by the UI of MyLifeOrganized (MLO), but focused on notes and thinking rather than task management.

title: Key requirements
note:
- Hierarchical (tree-based) notes with unlimited nesting, collapse/expand, drag-and-drop, focus on an item
- Runs on every device as an installable PWA
- Standalone first: a device works fully on its own, with no internet, no account and no server; pairing with other devices and server sync are optional and can be added later
- Synchronisation of items across devices over the internet
- Touch-first outliner UX for phone and tablet; keyboard shortcuts on desktop as a nice add-on
- End-to-end encrypted: notes are encrypted on the device before sync; the server never sees plaintext
- Fast full-text search across all notes, performed on the device (the server never sees plaintext)
- Direct device-to-device sync: two paired devices can exchange events with each other without going through the sync server
- Multiple trees per device: a device can hold several independent trees side by side, each with its own key and event log (for example a private and a work tree)
- See where changes come from: every device has a label (for example "Tablet"), and an item shows which device last changed it and when
- Explicit sharing: pairing another device of one's own and sharing a tree with another user are two separate actions; every tree shows whether it is private or shared, and with whom
- Usable where VPNs are blocked: file-only sync stays a full alternative, the user controls app updates, and the sync server can be self-hosted
- Readable export and import: a tree can be exported unencrypted as Markdown, OPML or JSON, and such files can be imported as a new tree or into an existing item
- Importing a tree into another: another tree can be imported into a tree as a new branch, keeping its history (union of their event logs, re-encrypted with this tree's key); the receiving tree keeps its name, theme and inbox; everyone who holds the receiving tree can then read the imported tree including its history
- Honest about protection: the app states plainly what it protects (content) and what it does not hide (that and when ThoughtTree is used)

title: Quality goals
note:
| Priority | Quality goal | Motivation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Reliability | No data loss, offline or during sync, merge, import, update or conflict; all devices with the same events and the same app version show the same tree; notes outlive app versions, frameworks and cloud services, so old data stays readable for good |
| 2 | Privacy & Security | Personal thoughts stay private: end-to-end encryption on the device, the server only relays ciphertext; minimal metadata, in particular nobody operating or observing the server learns where the user is; integrity of events |
| 3 | Usability | Outliner UX like MLO on touch devices: quick capture, drag-and-drop, gestures; keyboard on desktop; accessible (screen readers, keyboard-only use, contrast, scalable text); English and German; honest about what is protected |
| 4 | Portability | Runs on phone, tablet and desktop in all major browsers (Chromium-based, Safari, Firefox); installable as PWA, later as store app or package; server self-hostable without Azure; data never locked in (readable export and import) |
| 5 | Maintainability | Testable (replaceable time and randomness, device simulation); changeable without breaking stored data (downward-compatible events, format versions); manageable by one developer; one language (C#) across client and server |
| 6 | Performance | Trees with thousands of items stay responsive (targets in section 10) |

title: Stakeholders
note:
| Role | Expectation |
| --- | --- |
| Owner / developer (Sourceress) | A tool for personal thinking that is fun to build and maintain in C# |
| End users (initially the owner) | Reliable notes on phone, tablet and desktop |

title: 2. Constraints
note:
- Technology: C# on .NET 10 (the current long-term support release, pinned in `global.json`), Blazor WebAssembly as PWA, ASP.NET Core with SignalR on the server
- Must work offline; network is optional and intermittent
- Source control: GitHub repository `AdventureDevelopment/ThoughtTree`, private until the first release, public from then on
- Licence: Apache 2.0 for the whole repository; the name "ThoughtTree" is not licensed
- Dependencies may only use licences from an approved list (MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD and similar permissive licences), checked in the push gate; MPL-2.0 is also allowed for test-only dependencies that are not distributed (for example the accessibility checker axe); fonts may use the SIL Open Font License 1.1
- Single developer, incremental delivery
- Hosting: Microsoft Azure (developer familiarity), free tiers wherever possible; release 1 has no sync server and serves only the static app from Azure Static Web Apps (free tier), with a preview address for every pull request; once a sync server exists, the container image runs on Azure Container Apps, scaling to zero; target cost near zero for a single user
- The sync service (and the static app) must also be deployable by others on their own server, without Azure
- Server storage stays minimal: an append-only encrypted event log per account (one account per tree); concrete store (Azure Table Storage, Blob Storage or SQLite) is an open decision
- Development process: trunk-based development with short-lived branches: every change, by a person or an agent, reaches `main` only through a pull request; release flags (Microsoft.FeatureManagement) instead of long-lived feature branches
- Branch protection on `main`: no direct pushes; the push gate must pass; changes to protected paths (`tests/specify/**`, `tests/data/**`, the reference model, `*.verified.*`, `docs/**` including the ADRs and the invariant catalogue, `.github/CODEOWNERS`, the reviewer agent's workflow and prompt, the branch protection settings) need the owner's review through CODEOWNERS, and an approval counts only for the latest push; `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and the rest of `.github/**` agents may change on the approval of an independent reviewer agent (required check, runs from `main`, sees only the diff and the rules; the owner reviews them until it exists; a weekly digest issue lists every such change); other pull requests may merge automatically once the gate is green
- Agentic development: the system is developed largely by AI coding agents; the test harness is what keeps it in a working state and must be of very high quality
- CI/CD via GitHub Actions: every push to a branch runs the branch check, every pull request the push gate; a successful build on `main` deploys automatically to a test environment on Azure; promotion to production is a manual approval step

title: 3. Context and Scope
Business context
note:
- User interacts with the ThoughtTree PWA on one or more devices; every device works on its own
- Devices can exchange a tree's events directly as an encrypted file, without internet
- Devices can optionally synchronise a tree through a central sync service over HTTPS/WebSockets
- Other users can receive a tree that is shared with them and then work on it like the owner

title: Technical context
note:
| Partner | Interface | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Browser / OS | Service Worker, local store (IndexedDB; SQLite on the Origin Private File System only as a revisit option, see open decisions), Web App Manifest, Web Crypto API | Installability, offline cache, local persistence, client-side encryption |
| Sync Service (ASP.NET Core on Azure) | REST + SignalR | Push/pull of encrypted events, real-time notifications |
| Authentication (device tokens) | Bearer token | Identifies which account's event log a device may access; one token per device and tree, no user accounts |
| Other devices (own or of other users) | Pairing or sharing flow (QR code or typed code) | Hands over a tree's key and account identity; no server involvement in key material |
| File transfer of the OS (share sheet, AirDrop, Nearby Share, USB) | File download / file picker, Web Share API where available | Carries the encrypted export file between devices |

title: 4. Solution Strategy
note:
- **Blazor WebAssembly PWA** for a single C# codebase on every device
- **Event sourcing** as the core data model: every change to the tree is an immutable event; the current tree is a projection of the event log
- **Offline-first**: events are appended to the local store first, then synchronised
- **Sync by exchanging event logs** instead of whole documents, which keeps conflicts small and mergeable
- **ASP.NET Core backend** as a thin event store and relay (REST for push/pull, SignalR for live updates)
- **Domain project for the client, contracts project shared with the server**: the server cannot decrypt events, so it needs only the envelope, the export file format and the API data; all domain logic (events, tree, projection, conflicts, clock) lives in a client-side domain project
- **End-to-end encryption**: event payloads are encrypted on the device with the tree's key, handed over only by pairing or sharing; the server stores and relays ciphertext plus minimal routing metadata (account id, event id, sequence number)
- **Several independent trees per device**: each tree has its own key, account identity and event log; nothing is shared between trees
- **Deterministic replay**: every device orders a tree's events by hybrid logical clock and event id, so all devices compute the same tree from the same events
- **Touch-first UI**: the outliner is designed for phone and tablet gestures first; desktop keyboard shortcuts come as an add-on
- **Pluggable sync transport**: every exchange between two logs follows the same steps, independent of how the bytes travel; the Sync Engine talks to an `ISyncTransport` abstraction, with the server and the file as the first transports
- **No gaps per device**: every transport delivers the events of a device without gaps: a device never holds a later event of device D without all earlier ones; conflict detection relies on this
- **Device-to-device sync by encrypted file**: works without internet and is triggered manually; one device exports its event log as an encrypted file, the user hands it over (AirDrop, Nearby Share, USB), the other device imports and merges it. A native wrapper with automatic local discovery is a possible later upgrade
- **User controls when to sync**: server sync runs only when the user wants it: live (continuous, with real-time updates), manual (on request), or scheduled at times the user plans; the mode is chosen per tree and per device
- **Later distribution as a store app or downloadable package**: adds reliable background sync at planned times and control over updates, which a PWA in the browser cannot fully provide
- **Self-hostable sync server, one installation per server**: the sync service and the app are offered as one package that anyone can run on a server they trust; an app only syncs with the server it was loaded from, so its Content Security Policy can stay strict; using the hosted server and a self-hosted one on the same device means two installations, each with its own trees; each tree records its server as an event, so all its devices agree on it
- **User controls app updates**: the app checks for and applies updates only when the user allows it
- **Later option: sync through a cloud folder** the user already uses; the app writes the encrypted export file there, which looks like ordinary file sync on the network; needs the store app or downloadable package

title: 5. Building Block View
Architectural style: functional core, hexagonal shell
note:
- Domain (core): pure functions; commands plus current state give events, events plus state give the new state; no interfaces to the outside world
- Application: use cases and UI state; defines the ports it needs (event store, transport, crypto, clock, files and sharing), calls Domain and stores the resulting events
- Adapters: implement the ports (browser storage, Web Crypto, files, server and file transport) and their fakes for tests
- UI: Razor components that read state from the application layer and forward user input to use cases
- Server in the same style: Server.Core with its ports (store, clock), store adapters, ASP.NET Core as the outermost shell
- Dependency rule: dependencies only point inwards (UI → Application → Domain; adapters → Application); Domain depends on nothing; checked by architecture tests
- Navigation state (focus, selection, scroll position) belongs to a view, and the application layer allows several views at once, so a structure sidebar and later side-by-side panes on tablet and desktop need no rework
- The application layer offers view models shaped for display (for example: item with title, collapsed, has conflict, number of backlinks); the UI binds only to these and never references Domain types
- Taken from Clean Architecture: the dependency rule, view models instead of domain types in the UI, a structure that shows what the system does; deliberately not taken: interactor, input and output port, request and response model and presenter per use case, and entities with behaviour as the centre

title: Level 1 – System
note:
| Building block | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| ThoughtTree.Domain (class library) | Pure core: events, tree, projection, conflict detection, hybrid logical clock, command logic, validation; used by the client, the simulation and a later native app |
| ThoughtTree.Contracts (class library) | Event envelope, export formats, pairing code, API data; shared by client and server |
| ThoughtTree.Client.App (class library) | Application layer: use cases, UI state, view models, ports; no browser APIs |
| ThoughtTree.Client (Blazor WASM) | Razor components and browser adapters (separated by namespace), resources, composition root |
| ThoughtTree.Server.Core (class library) | Server logic and its ports, independent of ASP.NET Core |
| ThoughtTree.Server (ASP.NET Core) | Shell around the core: sync API, SignalR hub, stores (in-memory, SQLite, Azure), serves the client app |

title: Code organisation
note:
- A new project only for a real boundary: deployment (browser, container), sharing (client and server), or reuse (simulation, later native app); everything inside a project is separated by namespace and checked by architecture tests
- Inside each project, folders by feature, named after the glossary and the same in every project: `Outline`, `Relations`, `Conflicts`, `Trees`, `Sync`, `Sharing`, `Search`, `Export`, `Feedback`, `Settings`; cross-cutting parts (`Clock`, `Text`, `Versioning`, `Crypto`) in their own folders
- Shared build settings in the repository root: `Directory.Build.props` (nullable, warnings as errors, analyzers, banned API files), `Directory.Packages.props` (all package versions, checked for licences), `global.json` (fixed SDK), `.editorconfig`
- Tests are grouped by intent, visible in folders, project names (by kind: `Specs`, `Properties`, `Model`, `Compatibility`, `Simulation`, `Rules`, `Contract`, `Security`, `Budgets`, `EndToEnd`, `Smoke`) and a trait (`Intent = Specify | Secure | Confirm`), and the CI summary is grouped by intent:

```text
src/
  ThoughtTree.Domain  ThoughtTree.Contracts  ThoughtTree.Client.App  ThoughtTree.Client
  ThoughtTree.Server.Core  ThoughtTree.Server
tests/
  specify/   ThoughtTree.Domain.Specs  ThoughtTree.Client.App.Specs  ThoughtTree.Client.Specs  ThoughtTree.Server.Specs
  secure/    ThoughtTree.Domain.Properties  ThoughtTree.Domain.Model  ThoughtTree.Formats.Compatibility
             ThoughtTree.Simulation  ThoughtTree.Client.Rules  ThoughtTree.Client.App.Rules  ThoughtTree.Server.Contract
             ThoughtTree.Server.Security  ThoughtTree.Architecture.Rules  ThoughtTree.Performance.Budgets
  confirm/   ThoughtTree.EndToEnd  ThoughtTree.Deployment.Smoke
  support/   ThoughtTree.Testing  ThoughtTree.Client.SpecHost
  data/      formats/  regression-seeds/  synthetic-datasets/
infra/       Bicep templates
deploy/      Docker Compose example for self-hosting
docs/        architecture, ADRs
```

- Where tests of each kind live: Domain specs in `Domain.Specs`; invariants and properties in `Domain.Properties`; use cases in `Client.App.Specs` (Specify); privacy confirmations and language resources as rules in `Client.App.Rules` (Secure); generic component rules (test ids, accessible names, pseudo-localisation) in `Client.Rules`; UI and accessibility specifications in `Client.Specs`; store contract tests in `Server.Contract`
- `tests/specify/` is protected as a whole: specs may be added, changing or deleting one needs human approval; every runtime scenario of section 6 is covered by at least one spec that names it
- Specs are written with LambdaTale in domain language at every level (Domain, application layer, UI, server); end-to-end tests use LambdaTale too but confirm rather than specify

title: Level 2 – Client
note:
| Component | Project | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client Application Layer (ThoughtTree.Client.App) | Client.App | Plain C#: use cases (capture, move, resolve conflicts, pair, share, export, …), UI state (selection, focus, open dialogs) and UI decisions (for example: sharing requires a confirmed warning); used by the Razor components and by the simulation |
| Browser Adapters | Client (adapters) | Every browser API (local store, Web Crypto, file and share APIs, QR scanner, clipboard, service worker) behind a C# interface, with thin JavaScript interop implementations and fakes for tests |
| Outline UI | Client (UI) | Razor components that only show state and forward user input: tree rendering, touch editing, gestures, drag-and-drop, focus; keyboard shortcuts on desktop |
| Tree Manager | Client.App | Lists, creates, switches and deletes trees (the name comes from the projection); the only component that stores a tree's secrets and settings: key and `KeyId`, account id and secret, device token, whether this device uses the tree's server, sync mode; removes the key when a tree is deleted |
| Command Handler | Client.App (calls command logic in Domain) | Wires user actions to the command logic in ThoughtTree.Domain, which decides which events to write, with clock, `replaces` and `seen`; stores the result |
| Local Event Store | Port in Client.App, implemented in Client (adapters) | Append-only log in the local store; tracks sync progress per destination (server, devices synced by file) |
| Projection | Domain (pure); snapshots stored through a Client.App port | Builds the in-memory tree from events; incremental updates; snapshots; derives conflicts |
| Search | Domain (matching, index logic), Client.App (use case) | Client-side full-text search over the projection; optional local index |
| Crypto | Port in Client.App, implemented in Client (adapters) | Stateless operations with the Web Crypto API: creates keys, pads, encrypts and decrypts envelopes; stores nothing, the non-extractable key handle is handed in for each operation ([ADR-073](item:43633a32-ed5d-5734-b4af-16d4c581810e)) |
| Sync Engine | Client.App | Exchanges events through an `ISyncTransport`: push unsynced encrypted events, pull remote events, decrypt, merge and apply |
| Server Transport | Client (adapters) | `ISyncTransport` over the Sync API and Sync Hub |
| File Transport | Client (adapters); file format in Contracts | `ISyncTransport` that writes the encrypted export file and reads an imported one |
| Sync Scheduler | Client.App | Decides when to sync: live, manual or scheduled mode; scheduled sync at a random moment in a UTC window; batching of pushes |
| Pairing & Sharing | Client.App; QR scanner in Client (adapters); code format in Contracts | Creates and scans pairing and sharing codes; adds a received tree as a further tree, or imports a tree into another as a new branch (re-encrypting its envelopes, see Importing a tree into another); writes `device.joined`; keeps pairing and sharing apart |
| Conflict View | Client (UI) with use case in Client.App | Lists the conflicts the projection derives from the log and lets the user resolve them by writing the resolving event |
| Update Control | Client.App; service worker in Client | Checks for and applies app updates only with the user's consent; triggers rebuilding snapshots and search index after an update |
| Storage Guard | Client.App; browser checks in Client (adapters) | Requests persistent storage, warns when the app runs in a plain browser tab instead of being installed, reminds the user to export |
| Readable Export/Import | Client.App; formats in Contracts | Exports the current tree, or one branch from the item's actions ([ADR-080](item:5512e2ce-cc4b-5c03-9cca-340487536507)), unencrypted as Markdown, OPML or JSON; imports such files as a new tree or into an item |
| Auth Client | Client (adapters) | Attaches the tree's device token, held by the Tree Manager, to sync requests |
| Service Worker | Client (static files) | Caches app shell and assets for offline start; applies app updates only when the user allows it |

title: Level 2 – Server
note:
| Component | Project | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sync API (REST) | Server | `POST /v1/events` (push ciphertext), `GET /v1/events?since=` (pull), plus registration, tokens, capabilities, inbox and account deletion; versioned ([ADR-037](item:6b2c2a7e-542e-5ef5-aacf-272cf9336ea1)); the full contract is defined in Contracts before the first release with a server (open decision) |
| Sync Hub (SignalR) | Server | Notifies connected devices about new events |
| Event Store | Port in Server.Core, implementations in Server | Persistent per-account append-only log of encrypted envelopes; gap-free sequence numbers, readable only in commit order; a pushed batch is stored all or nothing (see Event exchange) |
| Registration | Server.Core | Registers an account on first contact; issues device tokens to devices that present the account secret |
| Account Capabilities | Server.Core | Stores permission and experiment flags per account (for example the private feedback inbox) and reports them to the device during sync |
| Feedback Inbox | Server.Core | Stores feedback encrypted to the operator's public key until the operator collects it; can be switched off by an operations flag |
| Auth | Server.Core (validation), Server (middleware) | Validates device tokens, scopes requests to one account |

title: 6. Runtime View
Scenario: Editing an item offline
note:
1. User edits an item's title in the Outline UI
2. Command Handler creates an `item.title-changed` event with the next hybrid logical clock value
3. Local Event Store appends the event; it is not yet known to any sync destination
4. Projection applies the event; UI updates immediately

title: Scenario: Coming back online (live sync mode)
note:
1. Sync Engine detects connectivity
2. Pushes all events the server does not have yet to `POST /v1/events`, batch by batch, strictly one after another
3. Pulls events since last known server sequence number
4. Applies remote events to the projection, which derives any conflicts; the user resolves them in the Conflict View
5. Server broadcasts new events to other devices via SignalR

title: Scenario: Real-time update on a second device (live sync mode only)
note:
1. SignalR hub signals "new events available"
2. Device pulls events since its last sequence number
3. Projection updates the tree

title: Scenario: Concurrent edits on two devices
note:
1. Device A and device B are offline; both last saw the change of item N's title made by event E1
2. On Monday A renames N to "Ideas"; the event gets A's clock (Monday) and names E1 as the change it replaces
3. On Friday B renames N to "Thoughts"; the event gets B's clock (Friday) and also names E1
4. After the next sync both devices hold both events and replay them in the agreed order; "Thoughts" comes later and is shown on both devices
5. Because both renames replace the same change E1, both devices mark N as having a conflict and offer both titles
6. The user picks a title on either device; this writes a new title change that names both renames as replaced, and the conflict disappears on all devices once they have synced

title: Scenario: Deleting an item that another device changed
note:
1. Device A and device B are offline
2. On A the user deletes item N with its subtree; the deletion records what A had seen from each device
3. On B the user adds a child to N and renames one of N's children
4. After the next sync, N is deleted on both devices, but marked as a conflict, because the deletion had not seen B's changes
5. The user sees the conflict, for example in a list of conflicts of the tree, and chooses: keep N deleted, or restore N with B's changes

title: Scenario: Readable export and import
note:
1. The user chooses "Export readable" for one tree and picks Markdown, OPML or JSON
2. The app warns that the file is not encrypted and anyone who gets it can read the whole tree; the user confirms
3. The app writes the current tree, without history, deleted items or device information, into a file whose name marks it as unencrypted
4. On any device, also one without the tree's key, the user chooses "Import readable" and picks such a file, for example an OPML export from another outliner
5. As a new tree: the app creates a tree with its own key, writes the same starting events as for any new tree, then the imported content; into an existing item: the content is written under that item
6. Every imported item gets a new id (except in an update import, step 8); `item:` links within the imported content are rewritten to the new ids; links to items outside the file are shown as not found
7. A JSON import also restores relations and their notes, tags and relation types (`relation.added`, `relation.note-changed`, `item.tagged`, `relation-type.set`; tags and types are items in the marked branches); the target keeps its own default type, and an imported `related` arrives as an ordinary type ([ADR-082](item:f593841b-7318-58f3-8ca0-6f42beea0253), [ADR-084](item:705c6e4b-83f7-5842-beb8-170c019a04e2)); the imported tag and type items move into the target's Tags and Relation types branches without matching, and equal tag titles get the offer to join (owner 2026-11-19)
8. Update instead of copy ([ADR-078](item:77cb2789-955d-5774-ad8d-96da9c92986e)): the export writes `item.exported` or `tree.exported` with the export point into the log, and the files carry each item's id and that event's id, no device information; imported into the tree they came from, the app offers "Update from these files", writes ordinary change events for known items (a change made in the app since the export becomes a visible conflict), creates new items only for unknown content, lists items whose files are missing and deletes them only after the user confirms, all as one action

title: Scenario: Device with a clock far ahead
note:
1. Device A's clock is three days ahead; it writes events with clocks three days in the future
2. Device B receives them, accepts them and raises its own clock to theirs, so its later edits still come after A's events
3. B warns that A's clock seems to be wrong
4. Until real time catches up, B's clock counts on from A's time; the order stays the same on every device, but edits are no longer ordered by real time

title: Scenario: Event from a newer app version
note:
1. Device A runs a newer app version and writes an event type or event version that device B does not know
2. Device B receives the event by sync or file, stores it in its Local Event Store and keeps it for further sync
3. The projection on B skips the event and the app suggests updating
4. After the update B replays the log again and the event takes effect

title: Scenario: First device setup
note:
1. User installs ThoughtTree and opens it for the first time
2. App generates a user id, with an empty user name; this is the user identity; nothing is asked, in line with [D-134](item:bab4aec8-1f8a-53c2-ae80-53520d3dd214) (first start goes straight into the tutorial)
3. App generates a device id and a device label from the platform (such as "Phone" or "Tablet"); name and label are asked for later, at the first pairing and in More › Settings, and can be changed at any time (owner decision 2026-11-16)
4. App creates two trees locally, each with its own key and account identity (account id and account secret) generated with the Web Crypto API and stored in the local store; nothing is sent anywhere:
   - the tutorial tree, written in the device's language from the app's resource files, which explains ThoughtTree by its own items; it is opened first
   - the user's own tree, named "My thoughts" by default (changeable at any time), with its inbox and the name item (step 5); no decision about a name is needed before the user has seen anything
5. Each tree starts with these events: `device.joined` for this device and user, the branch "Tags" with `tree.tags-set`, the branch "Relation types" with `tree.relation-types-set` and inside it the type `related` (`relation-type.set`, marked as the default by `tree.default-relation-type-set`, [ADR-084](item:705c6e4b-83f7-5842-beb8-170c019a04e2)), the inbox item with `tree.inbox-set` and the predefined theme "Inbox" (`theme.set`), and a first top-level item whose title is the tree name; the tutorial tree then contains its tutorial items
6. User works through the tutorial or starts taking notes; events are stored locally
7. No internet, login or server is needed at any point

title: Scenario: Creating another tree on a device
note:
1. User chooses "New tree" and gives it a name
2. App generates a new key and a new account identity for this tree, locally; the first event of the tree is a `device.joined` for this device and user
3. The tree starts with the same events as the first tree: `device.joined`, the Tags and Relation types branches with the type `related`, the inbox item with `tree.inbox-set` and the predefined theme "Inbox" (`theme.set`, [ADR-066](item:d47b0df5-b7f2-5735-83eb-8681e57b5f6c)), and a first top-level item whose title is the name; it is independent of all other trees on the device
4. User moves between trees with the tree switcher

title: Scenario: Pairing another device of the same user
note:
1. Pairing is for the user's own devices; it is optional, works without internet, and always concerns one tree
2. On a device that holds the tree the user opens "Pair another device…" (More › This tree…, UX decisions [D-187](item:6221eb17-41f9-5529-86f3-5d2387714723), [D-193](item:0055fe4f-8702-512d-9075-574046bf1f21)); the new device starts from "＋ Pair with a device…" in its tree list
3. App renders a QR code containing the tree access (see Tree access) plus the user identity, generated locally (also shown as a typed code for devices without a camera)
4. The new device scans the QR code (or the user types the code)
5. The new device asks the user what to do: add the tree next to the trees already on this device, or cancel
6. Add: the tree is stored as a further tree with its own key; nothing else on the device changes
7. Once the tree's events have arrived (by file or through the server), the user can import it into one of the device's own trees as a new branch ("Import 'Ideas' into 'My thoughts' as a new branch", see Importing a tree into another)
8. The new device takes over the user identity from the QR code and writes a `device.joined` event, so the tree knows this device belongs to the same user; if the device already had a different user identity, the app asks whether both are the same person, and if so the device writes a new `device.joined` with the adopted identity in each of its other trees
9. The devices now exchange the tree's events by file, or through the server if server sync is switched on for that tree

title: Scenario: Sharing a tree with another user
note:
1. Sharing is a separate action from pairing; it works without internet and always concerns one tree
2. On a device that holds the tree the user opens "Share with another user" and confirms a warning: the other user will be able to read and change the whole tree, and this cannot be taken back
3. App renders a QR code containing the tree access, marked as a share; it does not contain the user identity, so the other user keeps their own
4. The other user's device scans the QR code and stores the tree as a further tree next to its own; its own trees and its own user identity stay untouched
5. The other user's device writes a `device.joined` event with its own user identity
6. From then on the tree is shown as shared on all devices that hold it, with the list of users and their devices
7. Events are exchanged by file, or through the server if server sync is switched on for that tree

title: Scenario: Switching on server sync (optional)
note:
1. On any device the user switches on server sync for the tree; the server is always the one this installation was loaded from (the hosted service, or a self-hosted server whose app the user opened); the device writes a `tree.server-changed` event with that address, so all devices of the tree learn it
2. The device contacts the Sync Service with the account identity; the first device to do so registers the account, later devices prove membership with the account secret
3. Sync Service issues a device token for this device and this tree; a device that syncs several trees holds one token per tree
4. The user chooses the sync mode for this tree on this device: live, manual or scheduled; the dialog explains the trade-offs and preselects live
